title: How to Get Better at Satisficing as an Educator
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. borrows Herbert Simon's term "satisficing" -- doing something at the good-enough level rather than the optimal one -- and argues it is a core survival skill for teachers, given that doing the job "by the book" is hopelessly complex and impossible to sustain at full optimization. He offers two concrete methods. The first uses a stopwatch's lap function on repetitive bulk tasks like email and grading, both to build awareness of actual time cost and to deliberately trade some quality for speed, arguing that fast feedback (a one-day turnaround) is often more valuable to student mastery than slower, more polished feedback. The second reframes larger tasks (reading a PD book, planning a unit) by asking "what would this look like if I had to finish it in an hour?", which forces triage toward a book's core ideas via inspectional reading rather than exhaustive coverage. Stuart closes by predicting, correctly, that the reader's to-do list already exceeds what's possible, framing satisficing not as laziness but as a necessary discipline within the broader "life stewardship" project he's building on the blog.
points: Satisficing is reframed from a compromise into a deliberate skill: using a stopwatch's lap function on repetitive tasks (email, grading, feedback) builds awareness of real time cost and normalizes trading some polish for speed.

Fast feedback on student work (a one-day turnaround) is argued to beat slower, more "optimized" feedback for actually moving students toward mastery, which justifies satisficing on quality in exchange for speed.

The "what if I had to finish this in an hour?" reframe turns overwhelming tasks like a PD book study into an achievable inspectional-reading exercise -- introduction, conclusion, and targeted chapters -- rather than an all-or-nothing read.

Stuart names the core obstacle to satisficing as a mismatch between the perceived infinite standard of "doing it right" and the finite hours available, and argues the fix is to consciously choose good-enough rather than default into overwhelm.
quotes: Satisficing isn't my word. It's Nobel winner Herbert Simon's. It means, "Doing something at the good-enough level, not the optimal level." Few skills are as critical to the well-lived teacher's life.
On paper, teaching is an impossible job. So is administration. Doing education by the book in the twenty-first century is hopelessly Byzantine.
For tasks that require lots of repetition — e.g., responding to email, giving feedback on student work — click the "lap" button on your stopwatch app each time you complete a single iteration.

But for feedback to be its most effective, it also needs to be quick — like, I get the best results with student feedback when there's a one-day turnaround on it. But in order to do it that quickly, it means I need to satisfice on quality — so, I use a stopwatch.
Accept the fact that you won't arrive having perfectly read every word of the book (if such a thing as perfectly reading a book even exists).
Want to see my psychic abilities? Here goes: you've got more on your to-do list this week than can possibly be done.
